text:
The young man turned down an avenue that grew thick among the trees;
she made a long circuit there. She walked slowly, thoughtful, nervous;
with her parasol she bothered the grass at the edges of the meadows. She
was in an extremely perplexed state of mind. Despite her long
reflections, she no longer understood herself or her brother now, and
she no longer knew what to do with this Rafa, so devoted and so rich. In
the depths of her heart she also felt sad; love was consuming her,
melancholy rose from the depths of her being, causing her a kind
of slow suffocation. The day before she had been at Arrigo’s house,
because she could no longer bear to remain without seeing him; she had
found him absorbed and almost hostile. He had not kissed her, had not
allowed himself to be kissed; he had sought a thousand pretexts to send
her away, and, when near her, he seemed to be on tenterhooks. He had not
even wanted to hear Rafa spoken of; he had said to her roughly:

— Do whatever you like with him! I no longer care about anything.

And she had grown meek, had tried to caress him, had said to him:

— I shall have to see him tomorrow: give me some good advice.

Then he had begun to laugh, with a bitter, malicious laugh whose
meaning she could not understand; then he had begun to pace about the
room, agitated, scowling.

— You will see him tomorrow?

— Yes.

— Then tell him he is an imbecile! In his place I would already have
taken you.

— Why do you speak like that, Rigo? — she had asked him with tears
in her eyes. And he had shrugged his shoulders without answering. Then
he had begged her to leave, because his head hurt and he wanted to be
alone. But at the door he had taken her in his arms, had clasped her in
his arms passionately, and had pushed her out.

Later, toward evening, on the pretext of asking her father for some
information, he had come to their house, perhaps to see her for a
moment, to smile at her for an instant, after having been so rough.

And they had kissed again, in secret, with greater anxiety, in her
father’s house.

She could not understand him properly. Perhaps he was being consumed
by a foolish jealousy of this man whom, deep down, she mocked and about
whom she was making a calculation so different, so remote from love.
But she would have renounced Rafa a thousand times over if he had said
just one word to her! And why did he not want her? Why did he, with such
obstinacy, make both of them endure such wearing suffering?

Behind the gate she saw the automobile standing there; she ran quickly
to it and got in. The chauffeur had already been given his orders: they
set off in haste.

In the hot afternoon the countryside glittered like gold: a motionless
cloud of dust hung over the road; enormous carts, loaded with furniture
or merchandise, drawn by many horses in single file, obstructed its
middle and moved slowly aside, with a great creaking, at the signals of
the horn. When another automobile sped past, with shrieks of its siren,
everything, for a long stretch, grew clouded in a thick haze of dust,
everything: even the sun.

Rafa put an arm around her waist; she tried to push him away, but
weakly; she was no longer talkative or merry.

— You see, — she said, — I cannot trust you...

He obeyed and began again.

— Are we going far?

— Not very.

— Well, what have you to tell me?

— Not now; we shall talk afterward.

— Ah, afterward...

— Are you sad today?

— Yes, a little.

— Why?

— Because of so many things... so many things...

— Tell me about them, Loretta.

— No, what good would it do? In any case, you consider me a very
frivolous girl... I am here with you... you even have the right to think
so!

She was now mingling cunning with sincerity in a singular way, without
realizing it. The young man bent over her, almost to the point of
kissing her.

— Do not say that, Loretta; you know very well it is not true. I also
feel a profound respect for you: otherwise I would not love you.

— No, you desire me; that is the right word. But as for loving me,
that is quite another matter; you would not have me come here.

— Use the familiar form with me again, Loretta, as you did the other
times.

— Not today, not today!

— Then you do not believe that I care for you?

She shook her head, incredulous, smiling.

— Are you certain of it?

— Absolutely certain.

In a little over half an hour they reached a small village that spread
its white houses across the great plain, encircled by an almost dry
little ditch, with both its banks covered in yellow flowers among the
dusty grasses.

The automobile stopped in the square, and a swarm of barefoot,
shirtless urchins came running up, hopping over the cobblestones. There
was a small garden full of coolness and peace beside the little church;
a gilded sunburst blazed, struck full by the sun, on the church façade,
and it shone so brightly that it seemed to be turning; the parish
house, behind the greenery, had the shutters of its two windows partly
closed; from one hung a sheet, from the other a white-and-blue-striped
percale shirt. A large tawny dog scrabbled along the wall.

— Come, — said Rafa; — there is a little inn at the end of the village:
we shall drink white wine there.

— No; I want to go into the church, — Loretta replied.

— Into the church?

— Yes.

— Very well, let us go, if you wish.

The chauffeur went to the inn to wait for them; they crossed the
square, the little garden full of shade, and climbed the four steps to
the churchyard. Many urchins ran after the noisy automobile.

It was not late; all the sounds of the village could still be heard:
the blacksmiths hammering, the carpenters planing, the weavers working
their looms. A chubby little boy dressed as a cleric was reading a book
while seated in the shade in the garden. He looked at them and did not
move. Beneath the luminous arch of the main doorway, swarms could be
seen buzzing. They entered. The church was poor, but devout and bright
like the soul of a sower; through the tall windows the sunlight poured,
broken into golden dust. Only an old woman, indistinct in the shadow of
the colonnades, was praying with her face in her hands; but she was so
still, so firmly kneeling, that she seemed one of the church’s
furnishings.

The girl dipped her hand into the holy-water font and crossed herself,
bending her knee slightly. A drop remained on her forehead, clear as a
pearl. Then they walked all around the apse, looking at the paintings of
the Passion of Christ.

The cool air smelled of faded incense.

— Why did you want to enter this church?

— A whim.

She walked ahead with a springy step, almost so as not to make any
noise; her shadow stretched obliquely across the polished floor. She
bent her knee again as she passed before the altar, then sat down on a
pew in the shadow of the colonnade and rested her forehead in her hand.

The crucified Christ glittered anew beneath his silver crown.

— And what are you doing now? — Rafa asked.

— Nothing. I like it.

He leaned against the column beside her, slightly stooped.

— I love churches, — said Loretta, — and the singing and the organs in
churches.

Rafa looked at her for a long time, then said:
